Can Someone Give Consent If They're Drunk or High?
No. This is the key rule from the SafeBAE Peer Educator Training: IF SOMEONE ISN’T SOBER, THEY CANNOT CONSENT TO SEXUAL ACTIVITY.
Sober is one of the 6 Pillars of Consent. The Sober pillar means everyone involved has a clear mind and the ability to make thoughtful, informed choices. Alcohol or drugs can blur judgment, slow reaction time, and make it harder to communicate boundaries. If someone is inebriated, they can’t fully consent. And if you are, you can’t fully read or respect someone else’s boundaries either. Consent requires clarity — not confusion.
You can NOT get consent from a person who is under the influence of any substance — and it’s considered sexual assault, even if they say yes.
Think of It Like a Designated Driver
Most of us understand what a designated driver is. We know we’re responsible not just for ourselves, but for making sure our friends don’t drink and drive — because the risk of serious harm is real. The same logic applies to sex. Hooking up when someone is drunk can cause deep, lasting harm. So use the same thinking:
If you wouldn’t let someone get behind the wheel, don’t let them hook up.
If you see a friend trying to hook up with someone who’s drunk, step in.
Tell them to get the snap and follow up later.
If your friend is drunk, help them get home safely — even if they’re mad in the moment.
Looking out for each other is part of consent culture. Alcohol affects communication — the more someone drinks, the harder it becomes to clearly express consent, or to recognize whether someone else is consenting. While alcohol cannot be blamed for “causing” assault, it often plays a major role in unsafe encounters. You never want to risk it when someone isn’t sober enough to make their own decisions. Being sober means more fulfilling sexual interactions.

Can Boys and Men Be Victims of Sexual Violence?
Yes. Some people believe that men are incapable of being raped or even experiencing less violent forms of sexual abuse. That is simply untrue — men are victims of sexual violence too. It is important to recognize that ALL genders are vulnerable to sexual violence, and ALL genders are capable of harming others.
The Facts About Male Survivors
1 out of 10 rape victims are male.
Men are more likely to be sexually assaulted than be falsely accused of rape.
Over half of male victims of completed or attempted rape reported experiencing their first victimization before age 18.
Women CAN and DO commit sexual violence against men.
Sexual violence is widely under-reported across all genders, but especially among male survivors.
Why Male Survivors Stay Silent
Men who disclose to their peers are often dismissed because there is a prevailing belief that “men always want sex.” There is also a homophobic cultural idea that if a boy does not want to engage sexually in a given moment, he must be gay — which leads to men not being able to report or disclose when they have experienced sexual violence. Many teenage boys experience violence that is incorrectly brushed off as “hazing.” And it is important to understand that just because someone has an erection does not mean they are consenting to sex — it is a biological response that has nothing to do with consent.
Remember: compliance is not consent. If someone is pressured, threatened, or guilted into a sexual act — no matter their gender — that is not consent. Does the perpetrator being a woman change whether it’s assault? No. But it changes whether people recognize it as assault — and that’s exactly the problem.
How to Support Male Survivors
If a friend tells you they’ve been assaulted: believe them, take their words seriously, and let them share at their own pace. Avoid minimizing or questioning their feelings, especially because of gender. Do not pressure them to report — that choice belongs to the survivor. It is crucial that we open up space to allow young male survivors to feel safe in reporting, and to know that they will be protected, believed, and supported when they do. Boys and men have a critical role to play in ending sexual violence — it’s going to take ALL of us to change the culture.

How Do Survivors Heal After Sexual Assault?
For many survivors, the road to healing is long, nonlinear, and deeply personal. There is no right or wrong way to heal — healing looks different for everyone, so do what feels best for you with the resources that you have.
Reaching Out and Connecting With Others
Often in life we find healing in the comfort of our peers. Talking with others can ease the sense of isolation and help survivors gain tools to cope with the effects of sexual violence and work toward healing. Even if a person intellectually understands that they are not to blame for the assault, they may still struggle with a sense of guilt or shame. When a person can connect with others who support them, it becomes easier to fully accept that they are not responsible.
Reconnecting to the Body
It can be frightening for survivors to get back in touch with their body and feelings following a sexual trauma — but while the process of reconnecting may feel painful, it’s crucial to healing. Being in touch with your body and feelings can eventually make you feel safe, confident, and powerful. Techniques to try include mindfulness meditation, journaling, walking, being in nature, yoga, tai chi, qigong or other mindful movement practices, and artistic expression through all forms of art. There is no right or wrong way to practice self-care as long as you are doing it in a healthy way — self-care takes practice, and the important part is that you keep trying.
Creating New Boundaries
You may want to think about setting some new boundaries with yourself and others. Notice when certain people, places, or situations make you feel uncomfortable, frightened, or uneasy — these are requests from your inner self for protection. You don’t need to justify your boundary to anyone. If people don’t respect your boundaries, they don’t respect you.
Therapy Options for Healing PTSD
There are many options for healing PTSD (post-traumatic stress) that results from sexual assault, including cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure therapy, stress inoculation training, medicines, and EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization Reprocessing) therapy — a simple and effective therapy that can help your brain process traumatic memories differently. You can find someone trained in EMDR at emdria.org or emdr.com. Every person responds differently to different treatments, so it’s important to know the options and seek expert help.
We also acknowledge that therapy can be inaccessible for many reasons. Directories like latinxtherapy.com, inclusivetherapists.com, therapyforblackgirls.com, and southasiantherapists.org exist to help bridge those gaps. And if you need support right now: National Sexual Assault Hotline, 1-800-656-4673, or text LOVEIS to 22522.

How Do I Report Sexual Assault? What Are My Options?
Before we begin: whether or not someone decides to report doesn’t affect the validity of what happened to them. Reporting is part of the healing process for some people, but that doesn’t mean it is for everyone. Survivors decide how, when, and where to seek help — and it’s important to support, not shame, survivors regardless of what they decide to do.
Who You Tell Will Mean Different Things
A friend, family member, or trusted adult — someone who listens, believes you, and supports you, without pressure to report or take action.
A counselor or doctor — these discussions are confidential unless there is risk of imminent danger, current and ongoing abuse, or a court order.
A school staff member — many school staff are mandatory reporters, which means they may be required by law to contact law enforcement and/or file a report.
Your school’s Title IX process — filing a Title IX complaint must result in supportive measures for you, and may result in an investigation and disciplinary actions.
Your local rape crisis center — many communities offer free counseling services, confidential advocates, and legal support.
The police — this may start an investigation that could result in charges being brought against the person who caused harm.
If You Decide to Report to Law Enforcement
You may choose to see a healthcare provider to get an evidence collection kit (aka rape kit) done, usually within 72 hours. Your first reaction might be to want to wash your hands or take a shower, but it’s important not to, so that as much evidence as possible can be collected. Reach out to Sexual Assault Response Services to request an advocate to meet you at the hospital — we strongly encourage this. A medical exam does not commit you to report to the police. Even if you decide to report, you should still get privacy.
Understanding Mandated Reporting
If you disclose abuse to a mandated reporter, they are legally required to share that information with local Child Protective Services. Anyone who works at a school is a mandated reporter, and if you ask someone if they are a mandated reporter, they have to be honest with you. If you’d like to ask questions without triggering a mandated report, you can pretend you’re asking on behalf of a friend.
You can also seek help anonymously through the National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-4673. Whatever path you choose, whether or not you formally report, seeking support can be helpful to your healing process.

How Do I Support a Friend Who Has Been Sexually Assaulted?
The first person a survivor talks to can profoundly shape their healing. A supportive response can open the door to safety, healing, and resources. A harmful response — such as victim-blaming — can cause shame, isolation, and silence. Your role is not to investigate or judge, but to listen, believe, and offer care.
Start by believing. The best way to support a survivor is to believe them. Opening up about sexual violence takes a tremendous amount of courage and can be very difficult to do. How you respond to someone who discloses to you GREATLY impacts their process of healing.
How to Show Support
Believe them — take their words seriously. Doubt or skepticism can cause deep harm.
Listen — let them share at their own pace. Don’t push for details.
Do not dismiss their experience — avoid minimizing or questioning their feelings.
Allow their emotions — give space for anger, fear, sadness, or relief.
Do not pressure them to report — the choice of whether to report belongs to the survivor.
Review options together — offer information about resources, but let them decide what feels right.
Continue support — check in, stay present, and keep connecting them with help when they are ready.
What to Say — and What Not to Say
Try saying: “I’m so sorry this happened to you.” “You are not alone — I know there are people that can help.” “How can I support you?” “It’s not your fault.” “I’m glad you felt safe to tell me so I can be here for you.” “You didn’t deserve that to happen to you.”
Don’t say: “Why didn’t you just leave?” “Why were you there?” “Were you drinking?” “What were you wearing?” “It’s going to be fine; just move on.” “If it was really a big deal, why didn’t you tell me sooner?”
Remember that there are many different ways people respond in stressful situations — fight, flight, freeze, and fawn are the most common stress responses — and none of them are wrong. How someone reacted doesn’t invalidate what they experienced. And remember that rape is never the survivor’s fault; survivors never “deserve it” for any reason.
Finally, be strong and take care of yourself. Secondary trauma is real. One person can’t be someone’s only support system — it’s okay if you need space for yourself, and it’s okay to help them find a trusted adult, advocate, or counselor who can also support them.

What Are the Risks of Sending Nudes?
For many people today, being online is an inevitable part of life, and sending nudes, or intimate images, has become normalized. The purpose of this page is not to be judgmental or to simply advise you to stay off the internet — it’s an opportunity to provide guidance and discuss the risks, dangers, pressures, and consequences of sending nudes so everyone can make informed decisions. That’s the idea behind SafeBAE’s #KnowB4UNude campaign.
Know the Risks Before You Send
If someone shares your nude without your permission.
If someone uses your nude as revenge or to blackmail you.
If someone you didn’t want to see your nude sees it.
If you’re pressured into sending.
If you or the person who receives your nude gets caught and faces criminal punishment — it is illegal for anyone to share or receive naked or sexual photos of people under the age of 18.
Sextortion and Online Predators
There has been a significant increase in predatory adults posing as young people on apps, social media, and gaming communities in order to pressure young people for nudes for the purpose of blackmailing them — also known as sextortion. The FBI is investigating multiple cases of young people who shared an image with someone they met online, only for that person to threaten to share the image publicly if they didn’t send money. We strongly recommend blocking any contact from an unknown contact that escalates inappropriately and seeking help from a trusted adult.
If It Happens to You, It’s Not Your Fault
We want to be very clear: if you’re pressured into sending nudes or they’re shared without permission, it’s not your fault. This is a type of harassment, and nobody deserves to have their nudes used against them or shared without their consent. Even if someone is pressuring you, you don’t owe anyone nudes.
Laws surrounding nudes vary state to state, so it’s best to look up “intimate images laws” in your state. If you’re being harassed or blackmailed, or you see someone else’s nudes being shared, reporting to a trusted adult is always an option — just be mindful that they might have to contact authorities. You can also block the person, tell them it’s not okay, and report it to the platform. And remember the BAEcode: don’t send unrequested nudes, and don’t pressure someone to send nudes or share them without consent.

What Is the Difference Between Sexual Harassment, Sexual Assault, and Rape?
Sexual harassment, assault, and rape are all forms of sexual and interpersonal violence. Sexual violence is a crime typically motivated by the desire to control, humiliate, and/or harm — not by sexual desire. The three terms sit on a continuum of sexual harm.
What Is Sexual Harassment?
Sexual harassment is unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other unwanted verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature. It can occur anywhere: online, in the street, at school, or in the workplace. It includes offensive remarks about someone’s sex, sexual requests, pressure and threats, intimate image sharing, physical intimidation, and online harassment. Sexual harassment includes sexual assault.
What Is Sexual Assault?
Sexual assault refers to sexual contact or behavior that occurs without explicit consent of the person. Some forms include attempted rape, fondling, unwanted sexual touching (kissing, groping), sexual blackmail, sharing intimate images without consent, coerced sex, and any sexual contact with someone incapable of consenting. Sexual assault is used as an overall term for any kind of sexual violence.
What Is Rape?
Rape is a type of sexual violence involving non-consensual penetration or touching, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with ANY body part or object, or oral penetration or touching of another person’s penis, vagina, or anus, without their consent. State laws differ about what type of sex qualifies as rape vs. sexual assault — but rape is rape, and both date rape and stranger rape are legitimate. Most rapes are committed by someone known to the victim.
Every Survivor’s Experience Is Valid
We want to be VERY clear: any violation of another person’s bodily autonomy is unacceptable and should be treated that way. Survivors can often compare their experiences with other violations and downplay them, or feel they can’t be upset because what happened “wasn’t as bad” as someone else’s experience. That is exactly what rape culture teaches us to do, and it’s up to us to end it. There doesn’t have to be visible injury for an assault or harassment to be extremely harmful. Scars do not have to be on the outside.

What Are the Signs of a Healthy Relationship?
In a healthy romantic relationship, all partners respect each other and are independent. Each partner is an entire individual, not simply part of a couple or relationship. And in every healthy relationship, communication is KEY.
Healthy Signs to Look For
How do you know if you are in a healthy relationship or not? Some healthy signs include: open communication, quality time together, shared values, mutual respect, realistic expectations, ongoing support, a strong sense of trust, making shared decisions, feeling safe, accepting each other, having fun, healthy boundaries, mutual affection, enjoying spending time apart, respectful disagreements, and inspiring each other to be better.
Keep in mind that some healthy relationships can have “bad” moments, and some unhealthy relationships will have “good” moments too. Look at your overall relationship, and ask yourself:
Can you be yourself?
Are you happy?
If you feel uncomfortable, can you speak up without fear of being punished?
Healthy Relationships Have Healthy Boundaries
When communicating with your partner, it’s important to talk about boundaries — things you aren’t comfortable with. Remember that boundaries are limits that you set for yourself, not the other person. A good boundary would be that you aren’t going to go home with someone on the first date. Telling your partner they can’t have friends of a certain gender is not a boundary — that’s controlling behavior.
It’s totally okay to have feelings of jealousy or insecurity, but how you act on those feelings matters. Those feelings are just feelings — they will pass or can be communicated and met with reassurance. It’s not okay to dictate what your partner gets to do because of how you feel.
Remember to check in with yourself to make sure you feel confident that your relationship is a positive one and that you feel comfortable communicating with your partner.

What Are the Signs of an Unhealthy or Abusive Relationship?
1 out of 3 teens will be in an abusive relationship. Intimate partner violence is physical, sexual, or psychological harm by a current or former partner — and recognizing the warning signs early can protect you and the people you love.
Unhealthy Signs to Watch For
Some unhealthy signs include: guilt trips, withholding affection, isolating you from family and friends, using money to control, unreasonable jealousy, ignoring or excluding you, refusing to communicate, constant put-downs, humiliation, saying “if you love me, you will…”, threats, intimidation, manipulation, blaming you, lying and cheating, always criticizing you, and violence or threats of it.
Abuse can be physical, sexual, psychological, emotional, or financial. It includes things like gaslighting — manipulating someone into believing their reality is untrue — and love-bombing, an attempt to influence another person with over-the-top displays of attention and affection, like buying expensive gifts as an apology instead of changed behavior, or giving excessive compliments and then degrading you.
“Ride or Die” Isn’t Healthy Love
Loyalty shouldn’t come at the cost of your safety. Staying in a relationship out of fear, obligation, or pressure isn’t love — it’s control. Ask yourself: Can I speak up in this relationship? Are my boundaries respected? Am I free to leave without threats or shame? If the answer is no, that’s not healthy.
The Cycle of Violence
Abusive relationships often follow a cycle: escalating tension, an explosion, then apologies — where the abusive partner begs forgiveness, makes promises to never do it again, and tries to make it up to their partner. Then the cycle continues. This is part of why leaving is so hard: it takes on average 6 times for someone to permanently leave an abusive relationship. And leaving is the most dangerous time for a person in an abusive relationship, so safety planning matters.
If you are ending an unhealthy relationship, consider your safety and well-being first. If there has been violence, if you don’t feel safe, or if you’ve been persuaded to stay before, it is completely OK to end things over a phone call or text. You do not owe your abuser your physical body in any way.
Where to Get Help
National Teen Dating Abuse Hotline: text LOVEIS to 22522 or speak to a peer advocate at 1-866-331-9474. You can also visit loveisrespect.org. Everyone deserves a healthy, non-violent relationship — and abuse is never the victim’s fault.

What Is Bystander Intervention?
Bystander intervention is the idea that we can all step in to help prevent violence, harassment, or abuse. And stepping in doesn’t have to be aggressive or confrontational.
Here’s why it matters: in a problem situation, the average person only helps 20% of the time when others are around — and a bystander is present in about 30% of cases of rape, threat of rape, or unwanted sexual contact. It’s natural to not know what to do. But if one person gets involved, others are likely to get involved as well.
The 4 D’s of Bystander Intervention
Direct — Directly intervening in a situation: telling someone to stop a behavior, separating people, or expressing your disapproval while it’s happening. Consider the safety level of everyone involved, including yourself.
Distract — Distracting either the perceived victim or perpetrator: asking someone for help with directions, suggesting you go somewhere else, “I’m starving, let’s go get food!” Distraction is one of the best ways to intervene in a questionable situation, especially when you’re not totally sure what’s going on.
Delegate — Seeking additional assistance from a third party: getting a trusted friend to assist, telling a trusted adult, or enlisting a party host to remove a problematic person. Useful when you don’t feel well-equipped to handle the situation on your own or when things become more dangerous.
Delay — Checking in with one of the people involved afterwards: checking on the victim/survivor to see how they’re doing, or confronting the perpetrator separately. If something bad happens and you weren’t able to intervene in the moment, you are never at fault for the perpetrator’s actions.
Before stepping in, consider your safety, the safety of the target, and the anger or violence level of the harasser. It’s not about being a hero or putting yourself at risk — but it is about preventing sexual violence. And it’s better to risk being wrong about a situation than passively witnessing harassment.
Be a BAEstander: Follow the BAEcode
We’re all pretty familiar with the term bro-code, so we decided to flip it. If bro-code is having your bro’s back above all else, then BAEcode means you are committing to keeping an eye out for anyone who might need help, even if they aren’t your friend. That means: watch out for the safety of everyone, safely intervene if you see something sketchy, never pressure someone to do something sexually, always get enthusiastic consent, look out for people who have been drinking and help get them home safely, and change the conversation away from sexist or negative talk about people.
If you see something that doesn’t look or feel right, trust your gut and check in. No one can do everything — but everyone can do something.

What Is Consent?
Consent is usually discussed in the context of engaging in sexual activity, but it can really be about any interactions of any kind. The actual definition is “permission for something to happen or agreement to do something.” Put simply: consent = asking permission.
That means people can be practicing consent LONG before it has anything to do with sex. You should ask consent to borrow your sister’s sweater! Consent starts when you are a little kid — way back when your caretaker taught you to say “please.”
The 6 Pillars of Consent
In the SafeBAE Certified Peer Educator Training, we teach consent through the 6 Pillars of Consent and how to apply them:
Mutual
— Both parties agree to any and all intimacy without pressure. Consent is often framed as one person asking and one person giving, but that isn’t how it works in practice. Consent is about mutual experiences and collaboration, where all people involved get to voice their desires and boundaries and have them respected.
Ongoing
— Consent that is given one time isn’t consent to any time after that, and consent that is given for one action is not consent for all actions. Keep checking in throughout — communication is KEY, and checking in is the MOST effective way to make sure you aren’t pushing someone out of their comfort level.
Voluntary
— Consent is voluntary when you genuinely want to participate — freely, clearly, and without pressure. You’re saying yes because you’re excited to, not because you feel pressured, worn down, or afraid to say no. NO doesn’t mean convince me!
Sober
— Everyone involved has a clear mind and the ability to make thoughtful, informed choices. If someone is inebriated, they can’t fully consent. Consent requires clarity — not confusion.
Revocable
— Either party can change their mind at any time, for any reason. No exceptions. No excuses. No pressure. Anyone can stop, and they shouldn’t be made to feel bad.
Enthusiastic
— A hesitant yes is actually a definite no. If someone isn’t having fun, stop and check in. The BEST kind of consent is when there is reciprocal pleasure.
Some Key Reminders About Consent
Consent must be active, verbal, and enthusiastic.
Silence is not consent.
The absence of a “no” is not consent.
Buying dinner, paying for a movie, or giving someone a ride is not consent.
Going to someone’s room is not consent.
Consent is not possible if someone is unconscious or asleep, under-age, under the influence of any substance, or being manipulated or pressured.
Good consent is a practice — so KEEP AT IT! And remember to be kind, respectful, and considerate to all your partners.

What Is Rape Culture?
Rape culture is a collection of values, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors which trivializes or normalizes sexual violence. Examples include victim blaming, slut-shaming, sexual objectification, minimizing the impact of rape, denial of widespread rape, refusing to acknowledge the harm caused by sexual violence, or some combination of all of the above.
The term “rape culture” seems extreme to some people, but it is real and a major factor in allowing harmful behavior to continue in our society.
Where Does Rape Culture Start?
This is where rape culture starts: rape jokes, victim blaming, catcalling, “locker room talk,” not believing survivors, teaching how not to get raped instead of how not to rape, believing rape can only happen to women, rating people’s bodies, stalking, groping, sending or sharing unsolicited nudes, revenge porn, and facilitation with drugs or alcohol.
Where is this behavior learned? We learn rape culture from media and algorithms, rape myths, racial stereotypes, peer influence, victim blaming, and gender and sexuality beliefs — from films, books, music lyrics and videos, video games, fashion, and pornography. Imagery, word choice, and language matter. It’s not hard to see how degrading humor, marginalization, and gender inequity can lead to rape-supportive attitudes and behavior.
How Can You Help Shift to a Culture of Consent?
Create a culture of enthusiastic consent — only engage in sex-positive activity when there is ENTHUSIASTIC verbal consent.
Stop victim blaming — perpetrators are responsible for an assault, NEVER the survivor. A survivor’s sobriety, clothing, and sexual history are not relevant.
Redefine masculinity and challenge gender stereotypes — don’t buy into ideas which view masculinity as violent and dominant or femininity as passive, weak, or less valued.
Have zero tolerance — do not share intimate images of anyone without their permission, and let your friends know you aren’t okay with them doing it either.
Take an intersectional approach — rape culture affects us all, and certain populations, including transgender youth, Indigenous, Brown and Black girls, and people with disabilities, are most at-risk.
Listen to survivors — listen to their experiences, have compassion, and believe their truth.
Don’t laugh at rape jokes — speak up when you see people using “locker room talk” or sexually degrading terms or behavior.
Be an active bystander — safely intervening signals to the perpetrator that their behavior is unacceptable and may help someone stay safe.

What Is Sexual Coercion?
Coercion is when one person is trying to pressure someone to do something by using force, pressure, or threats. And here’s the most important thing to know: consent is not possible when there is coercion.
Coercion can be done intentionally or completely by accident, which is why it’s important to think about your actions and have open communication with your sexual partner. This can help them feel safe to say “no” without worrying about upsetting you or fear of anger for not agreeing to do what you want. People can be coercive in a variety of ways, such as guilting or pressuring people into doing things they don’t want to do.
“No” Doesn’t Mean Convince Me
Media often romanticizes “the chase” — where someone keeps pursuing after being told no. This framing treats dating like a game, where persistence equals success and boundaries are something to overcome. That’s not romance. Dating isn’t a game, and consent isn’t something to “win.” Part of practicing consent is being ready for and accepting when someone says no. “Maybe” and “I guess so” aren’t substitutes for “yes,” and asking over and over until someone gives in is not consent either.
It’s also important to think about pressure you might put on yourself — internalized pressure is as real as someone else pressuring you. You should never feel like you owe someone sex or that you should do it to make them like you, to seem older or more experienced, because they did something nice for you, because they might be in “pain,” or because you started and stopped.
Power Dynamics Matter
Sometimes coercion happens because one person has more power — they’re older, more experienced, more popular, or in a position of authority. Power differences can exist between young people, too. Think about a freshman dating a senior: age, social status, experience, popularity, and access all matter. When power imbalances exist, the person with less power may feel pressure to do more in order to seem mature, experienced, or worthy of attention — making consent feel less like a choice and more like an obligation. If you hold more power, you have responsibility. Let the other person set the pace, check in often, and be mindful that your position doesn’t influence their ability to freely say yes or no.
Remember: compliance is not consent. If someone gives in because they were pressured, threatened, or guilted, that was never consent.
